method: A capo clamps the strings at a fret, so it raises every open string by one semitone per fret and a chord shape keeps its fingering while the sounding key moves up. The tool works backwards: the shape key is the sounding key minus the capo fret, counted around the twelve notes. The sounding key is picked from the twelve standard major keys (C, Db, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, Ab, A, Bb, B) or the twelve standard minor keys (C, C#, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, Bb, B), each stored with its tonic letter and accidental so chord roots keep a musical spelling; the derived shape key is the spelling of its pitch class with the fewest accidentals. The seven diatonic triads keep their number and quality under a capo: in a major key I, IV and V are major, ii, iii and vi are minor and vii is diminished; in a natural minor key i, iv and v are minor, ii is diminished and III, VI and VII are major. Chord roots are spelled on consecutive letters from the tonic, so a chord can carry a sharp or flat that is not in the key signature, as with F#dim in G major. The capo fret is a whole number from 0, meaning no capo, to 12; blank, fractional, negative or out-of-range frets and unknown keys or modes are rejected with a message naming the field rather than defaulted. Open-chord positions list the capo frets 0 to 9 whose shape key is C, G, D, A or E in major, or A, E or D in minor. Partial and cut capos, alternate and dropped tunings, barre versus open voicings, the octave added by a capo on fret 12, chord extensions and inversions, and which shapes a particular player can fret are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A capo shortens the vibrating string at a chosen fret and raises the sounding pitch by one semitone for each fret above the nut, so the same chord shapes transpose up with the capo.

A fixed transposition preserves chord quality: in a major key the diatonic triads are major on I, IV and V, minor on ii, iii and vi and diminished on vii; in a natural minor key they are minor on i, iv and v, diminished on ii and major on III, VI and VII.

The conventional names of the twelve major keys are C, Db, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, Ab, A, Bb and B, and of the twelve minor keys C, C#, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, Bb and B, which spell each pitch class with the fewest accidentals.
First-position guitar chords in C, G, D, A and E, and in A, E and D minor, use open strings and few barres, which is why capo charts list those keys as the easy shape families.
